articles.title: Common artificial sweetener aspartame makes brain cells more vulnerable to stroke damage, mouse study suggests
articles.summary: A new mouse study indicates the common artificial sweetener aspartame could exacerbate stroke-related brain damage. The sweetener suppresses protective cellular signals and increases oxidative stress, leading to higher rates of brain cell death.

articles.title: Stanford scientists discover a seafood that can reverse signs of aging
articles.summary: A substance found in edible sea squirts appeared to reverse several signs of aging in older mice. Plasmalogen supplements improved memory and learning, strengthened connections between brain cells, reduced inflammation, and even helped the mice grow thicker, darker hair. Researchers believe the compounds may encourage brain regeneration and protect aging synapses.

articles.title: Escitalopram reduces impulsivity and anger in women with severe premenstrual irritability
articles.summary: A new study finds that taking the antidepressant escitalopram in the days leading up to menstruation reduces irritability, anger, and impulsive behavioral responses in women suffering from severe premenstrual symptoms.

articles.title: Free-to-play video games carry heavy financial costs for a vulnerable minority of teens
articles.summary: A new study shows that just 10% of adolescent gamers account for over 60% of in-game purchases. These heavy spenders are significantly more likely to exhibit symptoms of gaming and gambling disorders, regardless of their family's wealth.

articles.title: Survey reveals associations between Big Five personality traits and nightmare coping habits
articles.summary: New research explores how our personalities influence the way we cope with nightmares. The study reveals that extroverts prefer to talk about their bad dreams, while other traits are linked to unique strategies like rewriting dream endings.

articles.title: Rising loneliness among US veterans is closely tied to psychiatric burden and suicide risk
articles.summary: A new study indicates that loneliness is a growing epidemic among U.S. military veterans. With over one in five experiencing frequent isolation, researchers warn that this severe social disconnection is strongly linked to depression, PTSD, and suicidal thoughts.

articles.title: Study finds AI companions boost mental health while damaging offline connections
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence companions can improve a user’s mental health by simulating empathy. But new research reveals a hidden trade-off: as users grow closer to emotionally intelligent chatbots, they often withdraw from real-world human relationships.

articles.title: Scientists discover previously unknown brainwave chains that organize memory during REM sleep
articles.summary: A new study reveals that during REM sleep, the brain uses repeating chains of rapid electrical waves to replay and organize memories. The findings highlight how different sleep stages work together to store our daily experiences.

articles.title: Scientists find a weak spot in one of the deadliest brain cancers
articles.summary: Researchers may have found a new way to weaken glioblastoma’s defenses against treatment. Blocking a protein called SET prevented tumors from forming in preclinical models, while targeting related proteins made cancer cells more vulnerable to radiation. The strategy works by restoring activity of PP2A, an enzyme that glioblastoma cells appear to suppress. Human testing will be needed to determine whether the approach is safe and effective.

articles.title: Semaglutide might reduce how much people with alcohol use disorder drink when they do drink
articles.summary: A new clinical trial suggests the weight-loss drug semaglutide could help treat alcohol use disorder. While it didn't eliminate laboratory-assessed cravings, the medication significantly reduced heavy drinking days and overall alcohol-related problems in treatment-seeking adults.

articles.title: Fresh Memory, Stale Plans: Dependency-Scoped Validation for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory
articles.summary: arXiv:2609.03340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed LLM-agent teams can read the latest shared facts and still act on an obsolete plan. A planner may derive an action from requirement $r_3$, another agent may commit $r_4$, and an executor may receive $r_4$ without replacing the plan derived from $r_3$. We call this \emph{stale-plan execution}: state freshness does not establish that the plan authorizing an action remains valid. We introduce PlanFence, a dependency-scoped action-validation protocol. Plans cite the exact public records they used, and an executor validates only the record

articles.title: Comedy is funnier when it is easier to process, new psychology study finds
articles.summary: A new study in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology reveals that jokes, memes, and punchlines are significantly funnier when they are easy to process. This cognitive fluency helps our brains quickly make sense of unexpected humour.

articles.title: A longer exhale may push your brain toward bolder decisions
articles.summary: Slow breathing with a prolonged exhale made people more willing to take risks by changing heart activity and increasing the brain’s sensitivity to rewards. The findings suggest that something as simple as controlling your breath can directly influence how you evaluate choices.
